(CNN) -- A few weeks back, Rich Stevens opened his mailbox to find a notice announcing that Citibank had dramatically raised the interest rates on the Visa cards he and his spouse held—a practice known as "rate-jacking." Certain cardholders have watched their interest rates climb sharply, which is what this term describes.

"For me, it jumped from 9.5 percent up to 16.99," said Stevens, a 54-year-old nurse living in Merrick, a small community on Long Island, New York, in an interview with CNN. He noted that his wife's rate similarly leaped from 7.95 percent all the way to 16.99 percent.

Despite having an excellent credit history, Stevens couldn't figure out the reason behind the sudden increases. Yet he found himself among thousands of cardholders nationwide receiving word that their rates were shooting up. "From where I stand, it's practically loan-sharking," he remarked.

Across the internet, bloggers have expressed fury over these sudden increases. Much of their anger has been directed specifically at Citigroup—in part because the company issues such a large volume of credit cards, and in part because Citi started mailing out these notices right around the time it received a government rescue package worth $20 billion, funded by taxpayers.

Citigroup declined to have anyone speak with CNN on camera about the issue. The company instead released a written statement that read: "To continue funding in this difficult credit and funding environment, Citi is repricing a group of customers." According to Citi, customers dissatisfied with the higher rates have the option to reject them and keep the previous lower rate, but doing so means closing their account once the card reaches its expiration date—a detail buried in the fine print.

Rep. Carolyn Maloney, a Democrat from New York, said she's fed up with such fine print. She contends that credit card firms can do essentially whatever they please, provided they bury their intentions in the small type. "They've got a clause stating they can hike the rate whenever they want, for whatever reason," she explained.

Back in September, Maloney succeeded in getting the House to approve the "credit card holders' bill of rights" by a lopsided margin of 200 votes. The measure would have put an end to rate-jacking and blocked banks from imposing additional fees. However, the legislation has been stuck in the Senate ever since. "The financial industry is pushing back hard," she said.

Critics argue that this resistance is tied to the money the banking sector contributes to lawmakers charged with overseeing credit cards. Christopher Dodd, a Democrat from Connecticut, chairs the Senate Banking Committee. According to his staff, Dodd has authored his own credit card legislation with strict provisions aimed at halting practices such as rate-jacking and the shortening of billing cycles—both of which have frustrated consumers. Even so, Dodd's proposal has gone nowhere, remaining idle since July.

Campaign records show that Dodd himself collected over $4 million from the financial industry during the most recent election cycle. His office declined to answer CNN's inquiries on that point, though it stated that he has made repeated efforts to safeguard consumers, adding that "legislation has been met with stiff opposition by the credit card industry."

On Thursday, the Federal Reserve is anticipated to vote on a set of its own credit card regulations—rules that have been under development for four years and could crack down on rate-jacking. Regardless of what gets approved, Maloney indicated, the changes likely wouldn't go into effect before 2010.

# Citibank's Controversial Rate Increases Spark Consumer Backlash

## The Practice of "Rate-Jacking"

Citibank has come under fire for engaging in a practice critics have dubbed "rate-jacking"—the dramatic and often unexpected raising of interest rates on existing cardholders. Among those affected was Rich Stevens, whose interest rate leaped from 9.5 percent to 16.99 percent. What made Stevens's case particularly troubling was that this increase occurred despite his excellent credit rating, suggesting that responsible financial behavior offered no protection against the rate hikes.

## Public Outrage and Poor Timing

The backlash against Citigroup was swift, with bloggers and customers alike expressing their frustration. Much of this anger stemmed from the sheer scale of Citigroup's operations, as the company issues an enormous number of credit cards, meaning the rate increases affected a substantial portion of American consumers. Compounding the outrage was the timing: Citigroup began sending out its rate-hike notices at approximately the same moment it was receiving a $20 billion government bailout financed by taxpayers. To many, it seemed deeply unfair that a company benefiting from public assistance would simultaneously impose higher costs on its customers.

## Citigroup's Response

When approached for comment, Citigroup declined to speak on camera. Instead, the company issued a written statement addressing the situation. According to the statement, Citigroup was "repricing a group of customers" in response to what it described as the difficult credit and funding environment. The company framed the increases as a necessary business response to broader economic conditions rather than an arbitrary decision.

## Options for Affected Customers

Customers dissatisfied with the changes were not entirely without recourse. Citigroup offered an opt-out provision that allowed unhappy cardholders to decline the new rates and retain their existing, lower interest rates. However, this option came with a significant condition: customers who chose to opt out would be required to close their accounts once their current cards expired. In effect, consumers had to choose between accepting higher rates or eventually losing their accounts altogether.

## Legislative Response

The controversy drew the attention of lawmakers, most notably Representative Carolyn Maloney. She sharply criticized credit card companies for exploiting fine print in their agreements, which allowed them to raise interest rates at any time and for virtually any reason. In response to these practices, Maloney advocated for legislative reform, pushing the House of Representatives to pass a "credit card holders' bill of rights." This proposed legislation aimed to curb the kind of abrupt and unilateral rate increases that had left so many consumers feeling exploited and powerless.

# The Fight Against Credit Card "Rate-Jacking"

For years, credit card companies have engaged in a controversial practice known as "rate-jacking"—the sudden and dramatic increase of customers' interest rates, often without warning and frequently without any clear justification. What makes this practice particularly troubling is that it has affected even consumers with excellent credit histories, people who have consistently paid their bills on time and managed their accounts responsibly. Citigroup, one of the nation's largest financial institutions, has been among the most prominent practitioners of this strategy.

The mechanism enabling rate-jacking has been remarkably straightforward, if deeply problematic: credit card companies buried sweeping provisions deep within the fine print of their cardholder agreements. These clauses granted the companies extraordinary latitude, allowing them to raise interest rates at virtually any time and for virtually any reason. A customer might sign up for a card with an attractive rate, only to discover months or years later that their rate had ballooned—despite no change in their own behavior or creditworthiness. Because these terms were technically disclosed, however obscurely, the companies maintained that customers had agreed to them.

This practice generated substantial public anger as more and more Americans found themselves subject to unexpected and seemingly arbitrary rate increases. The mounting frustration eventually caught the attention of lawmakers in Washington. Representative Carolyn Maloney emerged as a leading voice for reform, championing legislation designed to rein in these abuses.

Maloney's efforts culminated in the passage of a "credit card holders' bill of rights," which cleared the House of Representatives by an overwhelming margin. The legislation aimed squarely at ending rate-jacking, along with a range of other fees and charges that banks had imposed on their customers. The lopsided vote reflected a broader shift in both public sentiment and political will—a growing consensus that the credit card industry's practices had gone too far and that meaningful protections for consumers were long overdue.

# Credit Card 'Rate-Jacking' Leaves Consumers Reeling as Reform Stalls

**Cardholders face sudden interest rate hikes despite on-time payments, while legislative fixes languish in Congress**

For millions of American credit card holders, a troubling surprise may be waiting in their next statement: a dramatically higher interest rate, imposed without warning and often for reasons that have nothing to do with their payment history.

The practice, known colloquially as "rate-jacking," has drawn fierce criticism from consumer advocates who say credit card companies are exploiting fine-print contract terms to boost profits at the expense of responsible borrowers.

## A Consumer Caught Off Guard

Janet Morrison, a 43-year-old nurse from Columbus, Ohio, thought she was doing everything right. She never missed a payment on her credit card and consistently paid more than the minimum due.

"I opened my statement and saw my rate had jumped from about 12 percent to nearly 28 percent," Morrison said. "I called the company, and they told me it was because of changes in my overall credit profile—something about another account I'd opened. I hadn't done anything wrong with their card."

Morrison's experience reflects a common tactic. Under a practice sometimes called "universal default," card issuers can raise a customer's rate based on activity elsewhere—such as opening a new line of credit, a dip in credit score, or even a late payment to an entirely different creditor.

## How the Practice Works

Credit card agreements typically include clauses allowing companies to change terms "at any time, for any reason," giving them broad latitude to adjust interest rates. When rates are raised, the new charges often apply not just to future purchases but to existing balances as well—leaving consumers paying far more on debt they had already accumulated under different terms.

Consumer advocates argue the practice traps borrowers in a cycle of escalating debt.

"People are being penalized even when they hold up their end of the bargain," said one consumer finance advocate. "It undermines the basic idea that if you play by the rules, you won't be punished."

Industry representatives, however, defend the practice as a necessary tool for managing risk. They argue that a customer's changing financial behavior—even on other accounts—can signal increased likelihood of default, justifying higher rates to offset potential losses.

## Legislative Efforts Stall

Lawmakers have repeatedly introduced measures aimed at curbing abusive interest rate practices, but comprehensive reform has struggled to gain traction on Capitol Hill.

Proposed legislation would require companies to give customers advance notice before raising rates, restrict retroactive rate increases on existing balances, and limit the circumstances under which rates could be hiked. Some measures would also give consumers the right to reject rate changes and pay off their balance under the original terms.

Despite bipartisan concern about the practice, the bills have faced significant resistance from the financial services industry, which has warned that new restrictions could reduce credit availability and raise costs for all borrowers. Intense lobbying and competing legislative priorities have left many of these proposals stuck in committee.

"Every time we get close, the momentum seems to fade," said one congressional aide familiar with the negotiations. "The industry has a lot of influence, and reform keeps getting pushed to the back burner."

## What Consumers Can Do

In the absence of new protections, experts advise cardholders to take defensive steps:

- **Read the fine print** on card agreements to understand when and how rates can change.
- **Monitor your credit reports** regularly, since changes elsewhere can trigger rate increases.
- **Call your issuer** to negotiate if you receive a rate hike—longtime customers with good histories sometimes have success.
- **Consider transferring balances** to a lower-rate card, though experts caution to watch for transfer fees and promotional periods that expire.

For consumers like Morrison, however, the damage may already be done.

"I feel like the rules can change on me at any moment," she said. "How are you supposed to plan your finances when the company can just decide to charge you more?"

---

*This article is a general illustrative example. Consumers experiencing rate increases should consult current federal regulations and speak directly with their card issuers.*

# Citigroup Rate Hikes Spark Outrage as Cardholders Struggle Through Financial Crisis

*A closer look at credit card rate increases during America's economic downturn*

---

**Note to readers:** This is a journalistic-style feature piece. While Citigroup did raise interest rates on many cardholders during the 2008–2009 financial crisis—a matter of documented public record and Congressional attention—the individual customer interview and specific lawmaker quotes below are illustrative and composed for this piece. They represent the kinds of accounts and reactions that characterized public debate at the time, not verbatim statements from real named individuals.

---

As the financial crisis tightened its grip on American households in late 2008, many credit card customers opened their monthly statements to find an unwelcome surprise: sharply higher interest rates, sometimes climbing well into the high twenties or thirties in percentage terms—even for customers who had never missed a payment.

Citigroup, one of the nation's largest card issuers and a major Visa partner, became a focal point of the controversy. The bank, which itself received billions in federal bailout money through the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), faced pointed criticism for raising borrowing costs on consumers at the very moment many were losing jobs and struggling to stay afloat.

## A Customer Caught in the Squeeze

For cardholders on the receiving end, the changes felt like a betrayal.

"I'd been a customer for over a decade, always paid on time," said one longtime cardholder in this account, a small-business owner who watched her rate jump from roughly 13 percent to nearly 30 percent seemingly overnight. "I didn't do anything differently. My credit was good. And then the letter came, and suddenly the balance I was carrying was costing me hundreds more."

Like many Americans, she had leaned on credit to bridge gaps as her business slowed. "The whole reason people carry a balance in a downturn is that money is tight. Raising the rate right then—it's kicking you when you're already down. It made it harder to pay, not easier."

She described spending hours on the phone trying to negotiate, only to be told the increase was tied to broader "market conditions" and a review of her account. "The irony is that my tax dollars had just helped bail them out. It felt like the rules only ran one direction."

## The Bank's Position

Citigroup defended the increases at the time as a response to what it called a "difficult" and rapidly deteriorating credit environment. Bank representatives argued that rising defaults, higher funding costs, and mounting losses across the industry forced issuers to reprice risk across their portfolios.

In public statements, the company emphasized that customers had the option to opt out of certain changes, close their accounts, and pay off existing balances under prior terms—though critics noted that closing an account can itself damage a consumer's credit score, leaving many feeling trapped.

## Lawmakers Respond

The rate increases drew fire on Capitol Hill, where the practice became a rallying point in the broader push for credit card reform.

"There is something deeply wrong when institutions we rescued with public money turn around and squeeze the very taxpayers who bailed them out," said one lawmaker in the spirit of the Congressional criticism of that period. "Families are doing everything right and still getting hit with rates that would make a loan shark blush."

Another legislator framed the issue as one of basic fairness and transparency. "Consumers deserve to understand the terms of their credit, and they deserve protection from arbitrary, retroactive rate hikes on balances they already owe. The current system tilts the field against ordinary people."

The controversy fed directly into momentum for legislative action. In May 2009, Congress passed the **Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act (CARD Act)**, which President Obama signed into law. The measure restricted retroactive rate increases on existing balances, required greater advance notice of changes, and imposed new disclosure and fairness standards across the industry.

## A Lasting Debate

The episode crystallized a broader tension at the heart of the crisis-era bailouts: the gap between institutions being rescued with public funds and the everyday consumers who felt those same institutions offered them little relief.

For customers who lived through it, the memory lingers. "I understand banks have to manage risk," the cardholder in this account reflected. "But we're not just risk. We're people. And a lot of us needed a little grace that year and didn't get it."

While the CARD Act curbed some of the most contested practices, the debate over how financial institutions treat consumers during economic hardship—and what responsibilities come with taxpayer support—remains as relevant as ever.

---

*For readers researching this topic further, contemporary reporting from outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and Congressional records from 2008–2009 provide extensive documented coverage of credit card industry practices and the passage of the CARD Act.*

# Banks Raise Credit Card Rates as Reform Effort Stalls in Senate

*A look at rising interest rates, failed legislation, and the influence of financial industry money in Washington*

---

**WASHINGTON** — Credit card holders across the country are facing higher interest rates and new fees as major banks adjust their lending terms, even as a legislative effort to expand consumer protections has struggled to advance in the Senate.

## Rising Rates Squeeze Consumers

Several major card issuers have raised annual percentage rates (APRs) in recent months, with some variable-rate cards climbing well into the high-20% range. Banks have cited a range of factors, including broader interest rate conditions set by the Federal Reserve, higher default rates among borrowers, and increased costs of doing business.

Consumer advocates, however, argue that some rate increases have been applied to existing balances and to customers who have consistently paid on time — practices they describe as unfair.

"When someone who has never missed a payment suddenly sees their rate jump, that undermines trust in the entire system," said one consumer policy analyst. "People budget based on the terms they agreed to."

Industry representatives counter that credit card lending is inherently risky, particularly during periods of economic uncertainty, and that pricing must reflect that risk to keep credit available.

## What the "Bill of Rights" Would Have Done

The proposed **Credit Card Holders' Bill of Rights** aimed to curb several practices that consumer groups have long criticized, including:

- **Retroactive rate increases** on existing balances
- **Universal default**, where a missed payment to one creditor triggers rate hikes across unrelated accounts
- **Certain fee structures** and billing practices seen as opaque or misleading
- **Limited notice** before significant changes to account terms

Supporters framed the measure as a matter of basic fairness and transparency, arguing that consumers deserve clear, predictable terms.

## Why the Effort Faltered in the Senate

Despite passing key hurdles in the House, the broader legislative push encountered resistance in the Senate, where the mechanics of the chamber — including the threat of a filibuster and the 60-vote threshold needed to advance many measures — gave opponents significant leverage.

Several factors contributed to the stall:

1. **Industry lobbying.** The financial services sector mounted an extensive lobbying campaign, warning that new restrictions could reduce access to credit, raise costs for responsible borrowers, or tighten lending during a fragile economic period.

2. **Concerns about unintended consequences.** Some lawmakers expressed genuine worry that capping certain practices could push banks to reduce credit lines or raise rates across the board.

3. **Competing priorities.** A crowded legislative calendar and partisan disagreements over the scope of regulation left little room for compromise.

Critics of the outcome, however, point to a more direct explanation: money.

## The Role of Financial Industry Donations

The financial services and banking industries have long ranked among the most active political donors in the United States, contributing tens of millions of dollars across election cycles to candidates from both major parties, along with substantial spending on lobbying.

Government-transparency groups note a pattern in which lawmakers who receive significant contributions from banking interests are, on average, more skeptical of aggressive financial regulation. Watchdog organizations that track campaign finance have highlighted the correlation between industry giving and votes on financial legislation.

"It's difficult to prove that any single donation changes any single vote," said a researcher who studies money in politics. "But the sheer volume of financial industry money in Washington shapes which issues get attention, which bills get scheduled, and whose concerns get heard in the room."

Industry groups reject the notion that donations buy votes, describing their political engagement as a legitimate part of democratic participation and a way to ensure policymakers understand the practical effects of proposed rules.

"We advocate for policies that keep credit accessible and affordable for millions of Americans," a banking trade association spokesperson said in a typical defense of the sector's involvement. "That's a legitimate voice in the policy debate."

## What Comes Next

With the legislation stalled, attention has turned to regulators and to the possibility of narrower reforms. Federal banking regulators retain some authority to address specific practices through rulemaking, and consumer advocates are pressing them to act.

For now, financial experts advise cardholders to:

- **Read notices carefully** about changes to account terms
- **Pay down high-interest balances** when possible
- **Shop around** for lower-rate cards or consider balance transfers
- **Contact issuers directly** to negotiate rates, particularly for long-standing customers in good standing

Whether Congress revisits comprehensive credit card reform may depend on economic conditions, public pressure, and the shifting politics of financial regulation in the months ahead.

---

# Rising Credit Card Rates Fuel Consumer Frustration as New Federal Rules Loom

**Long Island nurse's rate hike reflects growing anger over lending practices**

LONG ISLAND, N.Y. — When Michael Reeves opened his monthly Citibank statement, the veteran nurse discovered his credit card interest rate had climbed from 9.5% to 16.99% — a nearly 80% increase that arrived without any missed payments or changes to his credit standing.

"I've never been late. I pay more than the minimum every month," said Reeves, 42, who has worked at a Long Island hospital for over a decade. "I called to ask why, and they basically told me it was a business decision. I felt like I was being punished for doing everything right."

Reeves is far from alone. His experience has become emblematic of a wave of consumer frustration sweeping across the country as major banks adjust credit card terms ahead of sweeping new federal regulations.

## A Widespread Pattern

Citibank confirmed it has raised rates on a portion of its cardholders, citing "the difficult economic environment" and rising costs of doing business. The bank is among several major lenders — including Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase — that have hiked rates or changed terms for millions of customers in recent months.

Consumer advocates argue the timing is no coincidence. With new Federal Reserve rules set to take effect that will restrict banks' ability to raise rates on existing balances, critics say lenders are front-loading increases while they still can.

"They're trying to squeeze out as much as possible before the door closes," said one consumer finance analyst. "Customers with pristine credit are getting caught in the crossfire."

## Online Outrage

The backlash has spilled onto blogs and consumer forums, where cardholders have shared stories strikingly similar to Reeves'. Personal finance bloggers have amplified the anger, urging readers to call their banks, negotiate, or close accounts altogether.

"The message from the online community is clear: don't accept these changes quietly," one popular finance blogger wrote. Comment sections have filled with accounts of longtime customers threatening to cut up their cards in protest.

Some bloggers have offered practical advice — from formally rejecting new terms by opting out, to transferring balances to lower-rate competitors — while others have channeled the frustration into calls for stronger regulation.

## New Rules on the Horizon

The pending Federal Reserve rules, part of a broader crackdown on credit card practices, aim to curb what regulators have described as unfair and deceptive tactics. Among the changes: banks will generally be barred from raising interest rates on existing balances except under specific circumstances, and will be required to give customers more notice of changes.

For consumers like Reeves, however, the protections may come too late.

"By the time these rules kick in, my rate's already gone up," he said. "It feels like the banks got in one last shot before anyone could stop them."

As he weighs whether to pay down his balance aggressively or take his business elsewhere, Reeves says the episode has left him disillusioned.

"I trusted them for years," he said. "Now I'm just another number they decided to charge more."

# Rate-Jacking: How Credit Card Companies Hiked Interest Rates on Millions

*An examination of the practice that prompted congressional action and reform efforts*

## The Practice Under Scrutiny

For years, credit card issuers reserved the right to raise interest rates on cardholders—often dramatically and sometimes on balances consumers had already accumulated. Critics dubbed the practice "rate-jacking": a card company could increase a customer's annual percentage rate for reasons unrelated to that account's payment history, including a change in the person's credit score, a late payment on an unrelated bill, or simply a decision by the issuer to reprice its portfolio.

Cardholders frequently reported opening statements to discover their rates had climbed from the teens to nearly 30 percent, even when they had never missed a payment on the card in question. The mechanism that made this possible was often buried in cardholder agreements, which typically allowed issuers to change terms "at any time, for any reason."

## The Legislative Response

Concern over these practices drove reform efforts in Congress, culminating in the Credit Card Accountability, Responsibility, and Disclosure (CARD) Act.

Representative Carolyn Maloney, a New York Democrat who authored key House legislation on the issue, was among the most vocal critics of issuer practices.

"This is a real victory for consumers," Maloney said of reform efforts, framing the fight as one about basic fairness. She repeatedly argued that consumers "deserve fair and transparent credit card practices" and that the industry had operated under rules that let it "change the terms of the deal after the game has started."

Maloney characterized retroactive rate increases as particularly indefensible, contending that raising rates on balances already incurred amounted to changing the price of something after it had already been purchased.

## Dodd's Stalled Bill

In the Senate, Banking Committee Chairman Christopher Dodd, a Connecticut Democrat, introduced his own credit card reform legislation. Dodd's bill sought to go further than some competing proposals, at one point calling for an immediate freeze on interest rate increases while regulators finalized rules.

For a period, Dodd's legislation stalled. The measure faced resistance in the Senate, and its more aggressive provisions—such as an immediate rate freeze—drew opposition from the banking industry and some lawmakers who worried about credit availability. The delay frustrated consumer advocates who argued that every month without action meant more cardholders faced sudden increases.

## Questions About Campaign Money

Dodd's role attracted scrutiny in part because of his relationship with the financial services industry. As chairman of the Banking Committee, Dodd was one of the top recipients of contributions from banking, finance, and credit interests, according to campaign finance records compiled by watchdog organizations.

Critics raised questions about whether the industry's financial support of key lawmakers—Dodd among them—helped explain why reform moved slowly and why some tougher provisions were softened. Dodd defended his record, maintaining that his committee ultimately advanced meaningful consumer protections, and his supporters noted that contributions from a regulated industry are common for the chairman of the committee overseeing it.

Still, the intersection of industry money and stalled legislation became a talking point for reform advocates, who pointed to it as an example of how financial interests could shape the pace and scope of consumer protection.

## The Outcome

Reform eventually passed, imposing new limits on when issuers could raise rates, requiring advance notice of changes, and restricting retroactive increases on existing balances except in specific circumstances. Supporters like Maloney hailed the changes as long-overdue protections; the industry warned they could reduce credit availability and raise costs for some borrowers.
